newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia PM defends reshuffle, deputy soothes miners.
newsitem.headline: Russia PM defends reshuffle, deputy soothes miners.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Friday defended cabinet changes to a hostile parliament while his new first deputy Anatoly Chubais promised angry miners huge sums in back wages would be paid.

"The changes in the government have been prompted by the needs of the current stage of economic reforms," Chernomyrdin told the communist-dominated State Duma lower house, explaining last Monday's cabinet changes.
The reshuffle was ordered by President Boris Yeltsin, who blasted the cabinet for failing to end delays in wages and pensions which have led to worsening social tensions.

"One of the main tasks now is to restore order in the financial sphere and in the budget, which means restoring order in paying wages, pensions and normalising the system of payments," Chernomyrdin told the Duma.
The Duma was angered by Yeltsin's decision to give top cabinet posts to reformers, including to his chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, a hated figure among Russian conservatives.
Conservative deputies were alarmed by promises that the new cabinet would give a new push to radical market reform.
The Duma demanded explanations from Chernomyrdin on the changes, but stopped short of seeking the government's resignation or urging the Kremlin to cancel the reshuffle.
However parliamentary anger is a far lesser threat to the government than the growing discontent of millions of Russians who have not been paid their meagre wages and pensions for months.
Trades unions are planning a nationwide protest on March 27 to demand urgent steps from the government. Chernomyrdin has sent new cabinet members to regions where the situation is most tense.

Chubais was the first to leave, heading for Kemerovo to take part in a coal miners' union conference. Miners were among Yeltsin's most loyal backers in the early 1990s but are now disenchanted with reform.

Bearing a message of goodwill from Yeltsin and about $30 million in back wages for the Kuzbass region, Chubais, who is also finance minister, vowed to pay all wage arrears by the end of the year and clear the pensions backlog by June.
Playing down the importance of planned strikes on March 27, the 41-year-old economist told the miners the new government had solutions but needed more time.
"We (the government) will take responsibility on ourselves," he said. "And if the Russian people put their trust in us for a little while, then today's very severe problems will be solved.
"Now, as never before, we have a chance to turn the situation around in favour of the Russian people," he was quoted by Itar-Tass news agency as saying.
Russian workers are owed about 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, according to official figures, of which 10 trillion is owed by the state, which is struggling with low tax collection.

In Moscow, Labour Minister Gennady Melikyan met employers' leader Vladimir Kolmagorov and labour leader Mikhail Shmakov to discuss smoothing the transfer of money out to the provinces to pay off arrears and ease tensions before March 27, Tass said.
"We realise there is real hardship in the country but we understand also the enormous danger of rocking the boat any further, since events could get out of control," Melikyan said.
